# FM1Kit

> A Swift package for installing firmware on the M-VAVE FM-1 over USB-MIDI, from iOS and macOS. MIT licence, latest release 0.4.2, not affiliated with M-VAVE.

Part of Drew Robinson's FM-1 projects: https://fm-1.drewr.dev/ (see /llms-full.txt there for the others). Source, DocC documentation and changelog: https://github.com/ocean/FM1Kit

## What it does

FM1Kit speaks the FM-1's firmware update protocol. It reads `.fwsc` firmware packages, finds the device, answers its read requests while it stages and writes the new firmware, and checks the device reports the new firmware afterwards. It can also finish an update that was cut off, or one started from USB recovery mode. It arms M-VAVE's open firmware before updating it, and after installing V15 it can rewrite the four voice banks with V15's 128 factory voices. Before switching away from open firmware, it can back up open firmware's projects and sample bank.

It sticks to the device. Finding and downloading firmwares is left to the app using it (FM-SWITCH does that: https://fm-1.drewr.dev/fm-switch/).

Tested on one FM-1 so far, from a Mac: installing M-VAVE's official V15, Felucca 1.6.1, Estampie 0.1 and M-VAVE's open firmware V12, switching between them, pulling the cable part-way through writing and resuming, restoring V15's factory voices, backing up open firmware, installing m-bootloader, and backing up, restoring and writing the whole flash in download mode.

## Requirements

- iOS 17 or macOS 14
- Swift 6.1 or later (Xcode 16.3 or later)
- An FM-1 connected by USB: an iPhone or iPad's USB-C port, a Lightning device through Apple's camera adapter, or a Mac

## Installation

```swift
dependencies: [
    .package(url: "https://github.com/ocean/FM1Kit.git", .upToNextMinor(from: "0.4.2")),
]
```

Until 1.0, minor versions may change the API, so this takes 0.4.x fixes but not 0.5.0.

## Usage

```swift
import FM1Kit
import Foundation

// Read a firmware package and see what it is.
let package = try FwscPackage(data: Data(contentsOf: fileURL))
print(package.product, package.sha256)

// Check what installing it would do. Switching to a different firmware can erase the
// FM-1's projects and samples, so it needs confirming once they're backed up.
let updater = FM1Updater(transport: try CoreMIDITransport(clientName: "My App"))
let check = try await updater.check(package)
let confirmed = check.kind != .switchingFirmware || askToSwitch(from: check.device)

// Install it on the connected FM-1.
let options = InstallOptions(confirmsSwitchingFirmware: confirmed)
try await updater.install(package, options: options) { event in
    switch event {
    case .staging(let requests): print("Preparing… \(requests)")
    case .writing(let fraction, _): print("Writing \(Int(fraction * 100))%")
    case .checking(let fraction, _): print("Checking \(Int(fraction * 100))%")
    case .finished(let identity): print("Now running \(identity)")
    default: break
    }
}

// Finish an update that was cut off, or one started in USB recovery mode.
if let identity = await updater.identify(), identity.isLoader {
    try await updater.resume(package)
}
```

`check.kind` is an `InstallKind`: `update` (a different build of the open firmware running), `switchingFirmware` (confirmed with `InstallOptions.confirmsSwitchingFirmware`), `sameIdentity` (the identity a custom firmware already reports, confirmed with `InstallOptions.confirmsSameIdentity`), or `reinstall` (V15 over itself, or the open firmware build already running), which isn't installed.

Each firmware brings its own update loader, and loaders write differently. Writing progress counts the firmware's application area, which every loader seen writes, whatever order it reads in (V15's reads backwards). Some loaders (Felucca's) then read it a second time, which FM1Kit reports as `.checking`, so progress displays should allow for an optional second step.

## Restoring V15's factory voices

Installing V15 over custom firmware can leave a voice bank holding the old firmware's voices. After installing V15, `FM1Updater.restoreFactoryVoices(from:progress:)` rewrites its four voice banks with the 128 factory voices from the V15 package, as M-VAVE's updater does.

## Backing up open firmware

`FM1Updater.backUpOpenFirmware(progress:)` reads an FM-1 running M-VAVE's open firmware through its project library: the 16 project slots, the project being edited (including unsaved changes) and the sample bank. The firmware can only read the project being edited, so each slot is loaded in turn and the workspace is put back afterwards. No slot is saved and the sample bank isn't written, but the FM-1's current project changes while it runs, so the person shouldn't play or edit until it finishes.

`OpenFirmwareBackup.write(to:)` saves the backup as `workspace.fm1`, `slot-NN.fm1` for each slot that isn't empty, `samples.fm1s` and a `backup.json` describing them. The `.fm1` and `.fm1s` files are the formats M-VAVE's workbench reads, so it can restore them. FM1Kit can't restore a backup yet, and Open V13's per-slot tuning tables aren't included yet.

Other firmwares (V15, Felucca, Estampie and the rest) have no known way to read their data, and each firmware stores it in its own format, so only open firmware can be backed up, and a backup is only for putting back on open firmware.

## Installing m-bootloader

m-bootloader (https://github.com/jvitkauskas/m-bootloader, MIT) replaces M-VAVE's bootloader with one that has a recovery menu (hold PLAY while switching on), the chip's USB download mode (hold REC), and checks the firmware before starting it. `BootloaderInstaller` reads its `fm1-uboot.fwsc` package, which holds only an installer, and `FM1Updater.installBootloader(_:events:)` installs it from V15 over USB-MIDI, keeping the firmware. FM1Kit can't read the bootloader back over USB-MIDI, so the FM-1's screen confirms the result. Installing V15 later puts M-VAVE's bootloader back. Firmwares built on Felucca's platform (AMB-1, HYP-1, DUB-1, Estampie) install M-VAVE's packages only over M-VAVE's own bootloader, so with m-bootloader installed they refuse V15 and the install stops with `FM1UpdateError.bootloaderMismatch`; going back to V15 from them then needs download mode, from a Mac. `FwscPackage.usesFeluccaUpdateCode` says whether a package's firmware is one of them, so apps can warn before installing it. Using download mode needs a computer (M-Flasher or FM1Rescue).

## Friendly progress, advice and device summaries

- `InstallProgress` folds an install's `UpdateEvent`s into one bar from 0 to 1 that never goes backwards, with four stages: getting ready, installing, checking and restarting.
- `FM1Advice(for: error)` turns any error into a headline, an explanation, whether the FM-1 is still fine as it is, one action (try again, resume, reconnect, switch off and on, confirm, choose another firmware, hold keys at power-on, needs a computer, dismiss) and technical details.
- `FM1Updater.summary()` returns an `FM1DeviceSummary`: the firmware's name and version for V15 and open firmware, whether it's waiting part-way through an update, and its USB serial number (V15 and open firmware report one; Felucca doesn't).

## FM1Rescue: download mode (macOS only)

The package's second library uses the chip's USB download mode, which works even when the firmware won't start. In download mode the FM-1 is a USB disk (4C4A:8057, "WL82 UBOOT1.00"); taking it from macOS's disk driver needs root, so FM1Rescue is macOS-only and empty on iOS. `FM1Updater.enterDownloadMode()` asks V15 or Felucca to switch with the MIDI message F0 22 24 35 7D F7 (with m-bootloader, holding REC while switching on does the same). `USBDownloadModeConnection.open()` captures the device with IOUSBHost and speaks USB mass storage's Bulk-Only Transport. `FlashSession` uploads m-bootloader's flash loader (bundled, MIT) into the chip's RAM and reads the flash, and `backUp(progress:)` reads the 1 MB twice and checks both against the chip's CRC-32. `FlashBackup.write(to:)` saves it as M-Flasher does (a .bin and a .json with the flash chip's unique ID), and `FlashBackup.mBootloader` says whether m-bootloader is in the boot area, and `FlashBackup.firmware` whether the firmware's files are whole, which identities its code names and whether it's V15 (`name` also knows Felucca 1.6.1 and AMB-1 1.3). `FlashBackup(contentsOf:)` reads a saved backup. `FlashPlan` works out a change before anything is written, against a backup just read in the same session: `restoring(_:onto:)` puts a backup back (another FM-1's keeps this one's factory data, the last 4 KB sector, by the flash chip's unique ID), `installing(_:onto:)` installs m-bootloader from its `.boot` file (only the bootloader and its record in the 16 KB boot area change; the unit's boot configuration stays), `installingBootloader(from:onto:)` puts M-VAVE's bootloader back from a firmware package, and `installing(_:onto:includingBootloader:erasingSettings:)` writes a firmware package's image, refusing one not made for the chip key. A plan lists the 4 KB sectors that change, with notes and warnings, and `FlashSession.write(_:progress:)` checks the flash is still what was read, erases and writes only those sectors, checks each run against the chip's CRC-32 (writing it once more if needed) and shows progress on the FM-1's screen. Save the plan's `original` first: it's the way back. `SimulatedDownloadMode` simulates the chip, erasing and writing as NOR flash does.

## Types

- `FwscPackage` (struct): reads a `.fwsc` package: its identity, the image the device reads, and its SHA-256. Checks the header, target chip, per-part checksums, and that it holds a firmware image and an update loader, refusing a damaged or wrong file before anything is sent.
- `OfficialFirmware` (struct): recognises M-VAVE's official releases (V15 and Open V12) by size and checksum.
- `FM1Identity` (struct): parses what a device reports, e.g. `FM-1_916`, or `ota-FM-1_015` for the update loader.
- `FM1Updater` (actor): finds the device, checks and installs, resumes, restores V15's voices, backs up open firmware, and reports progress as `UpdateEvent`s.
- `InstallCheck`, `InstallKind`, `InstallOptions`: what an install would do, and confirming a switch of firmware or an install of the identity already running.
- `UpdateEvent` (enum): connected, staging, waiting for the loader, loader found, writing, checking, rebooting and finished.
- `FM1UpdateError` (enum): why an install, resume or backup stopped, with a description for each.
- `FM1Capability`, `FM1BuildID` (structs): what M-VAVE's open firmware reports, and the build ID it's armed with before an update.
- `OpenFirmwareBackup`, `OpenFirmwareProject` (structs): a backup of open firmware's projects and samples, and its `.fm1` project files.
- `BootloaderInstaller`, `BootloaderImage` (structs): m-bootloader's installer package, and the bootloader it carries (or a `.boot` file).
- `InstallProgress`, `FM1Advice`, `FM1DeviceSummary` (structs): one progress bar, plain advice for any error, and the connected FM-1 in plain terms.
- `CoreMIDITransport` (class): CoreMIDI connections to real devices.
- `SimulatedFM1` (class): a software FM-1 that speaks the update protocol and open firmware's project library, for the iOS Simulator and tests.

## Safety rules it enforces

Before installing, FM1Kit makes sure exactly one FM-1 answers, and won't reinstall V15 over itself. It installs a different firmware, or the identity a custom firmware already reports (a reinstall, or another release of a firmware that keeps one identity), only when told the person updating has confirmed it, as M-VAVE's own updater does. Switching firmware can erase the FM-1's projects and samples. Open firmware is armed with the package's build ID before it's updated.

## fm1probe

A Mac command-line tool for checking a setup and watching an install closely. Only `install`, `install-bootloader` and `restore-voices` write to the device, and `backup` changes which project open firmware shows while it reads; each asks you to type YES first:

```sh
swift run fm1probe ports                 # list MIDI ports and which would be probed
swift run fm1probe identify --repeat 20  # ask the connected FM-1 what it's running, 20 times
swift run fm1probe monitor 30            # print any SysEx the FM-1 sends for 30 s
swift run fm1probe watch 60              # show ports as devices come and go
swift run fm1probe inspect FILE.fwsc     # show a package's identity, size and checksum, or a .bin backup's firmware
swift run fm1probe install FILE.fwsc     # install a firmware (--resume, --simulated, --log FILE, --build-id HEX)
swift run fm1probe restore-voices FM-1.fwsc  # rewrite V15's voice banks with its factory voices
swift run fm1probe backup FOLDER         # save open firmware's projects and sample bank to a new folder
swift run fm1probe install-bootloader fm1-uboot.fwsc  # install m-bootloader from V15
swift run fm1probe download-mode         # ask V15 or Felucca to restart into download mode
sudo .build/debug/fm1probe flash-backup FOLDER  # read the whole flash in download mode (after swift build)
sudo .build/debug/fm1probe flash-restore BACKUP.bin FOLDER     # put a backup back, saving the flash to FOLDER first
sudo .build/debug/fm1probe flash-bootloader fm1-uboot.boot FOLDER  # install m-bootloader (or M-VAVE's, from FM-1.fwsc)
sudo .build/debug/fm1probe flash-install FILE.fwsc FOLDER      # install a firmware in download mode
```

## What an install looks like

About 20 seconds for V15 and under 40 for Felucca 1.6.1. The FM-1 first checks the package while running its current firmware, then restarts into its update loader, which shows up as a MIDI port with a new name (such as `Felucca Update`) and reports itself as `ota-` followed by the firmware's name, for example `ota-FM-1_015` for V15. After open firmware is armed, its loader instead reports the build it was armed with, such as `ota-FM1C_db1642b2b6fa5c2c`. The loader may leave the screen blank. If the update is cut off, the FM-1 waits in its loader until an update finishes, and `resume` picks it up.

## Recovery

Some firmwares can start in USB recovery mode: hold OCT− while switching on. Many don't offer it, including V15 and Felucca 1.6.1, and it can't help if the firmware is too damaged to start. Whenever the FM-1 is in its update loader, `FM1Updater.resume(_:events:)` can install a firmware. Beyond that is the chip's ROM bootloader from a computer, which FM1Kit doesn't cover.

## Credits and licence

The protocol is written from the FM-1-RE reverse-engineering notes (https://github.com/AL-255/FM-1-RE, WTFPL). Arming open firmware, restoring V15's voices and backing up open firmware follow the protocols as M-VAVE's open-source firmware and updater (fm1_open, https://github.com/m-vave/fm1_open) use them; package checks follow kagaimiq's MIT-licensed jl-misctools. FM1Kit contains no code from GPL-licensed installers and doesn't include M-VAVE's firmware (get it from https://www.m-vave.com/download). MIT licence.
